stages.name: Principal-agent problem
stages.title: Principal-agent problem
stages.sub: Why the people who own a company and the people who run it can end up pulling in different directions.

steps.q: A company has thousands of shareholders scattered across the country, none owning enough shares to run the business day to day. So who actually makes the daily decisions?
steps.wrong: The shareholders themselves, by voting daily
steps.hint: Could thousands of small shareholders realistically turn up and run the factory each morning?

steps.q: The shareholders own the firm but cannot run it themselves, so they bring in a manager to make decisions on their behalf. What is that manager now doing for the owners?
steps.right: Acting on their behalf as their agent
steps.wrong: Taking over ownership of their shares
steps.hint: The owners still own the firm; they've just handed over the job of running it. What role does the manager now hold?

steps.q: This hired manager sees every deal, cost and problem inside the firm as it happens, while the shareholders only see the yearly report. Do both sides know the same amount about how the firm is really doing?
steps.right: No, the manager knows far more
steps.wrong: Yes, they both know the same
steps.hint: Who is actually sitting in the building making the decisions each day?

steps.q: A manager's bonus and reputation grow when the firm gets bigger, even if profit per pound invested falls. Shareholders just want more profit on their shares. Do manager and shareholder want the exact same thing here?
steps.wrong: Yes, bigger firm always means more profit for both
steps.hint: Whose reward depends on the firm's size, and whose depends on the profit it earns?

steps.q: A manager pushes to take over rival firms and expand into new countries, even though shareholders think the extra profit won't cover the cost. Why might the manager still want this?
steps.right: It makes the firm bigger and more dominant
steps.wrong: It is the option most likely to raise profit
steps.hint: Think about what the manager gains personally from running a larger, more powerful firm, separate from the profit numbers.

steps.q: The manager (agent) knows more than the shareholders (owners) and wants different things from them. Given this, will the manager reliably act exactly as the owners wish?
steps.right: No, they may act in their own interest instead
steps.wrong: Yes, hiring them guarantees they follow owners' wishes
steps.hint: If the agent knows more than the owner and wants different things, can the owner be sure the agent obeys?
